fixes.answer: To me, living sustainably means meeting our own needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. In practice, it involves being mindful of our consumption, reducing waste, and using resources efficiently and responsibly. It is about living within the planet's ecological limits rather than [[depleting]] them. Essentially, it is a shift from a throwaway, [[exploitative]] mindset to one of [[stewardship]] and long-term responsibility.
fixes.why: 'responsibility' is plain and 'throwaway' used elsewhere; marked 'depleting' and 'exploitative'

fixes.answer: Yes, considerably so. Environmental awareness has grown enormously over recent decades, driven by scientific evidence, media coverage and visible impacts like extreme weather. Concepts like recycling, carbon footprints and sustainability are now part of everyday conversation, which was not the case a generation ago. However, I would add that awareness does not always [[translate into action]]. So people are certainly more [[conscious]], even if their behaviour has not fully [[caught up]].
fixes.why: 'behaviour' is plain; marked 'translate into action' and 'caught up'

fixes.answer: Several barriers make it difficult. Sustainable options are sometimes more expensive or less convenient than the alternatives, so cost and habit get in the way. Many people also feel their individual actions are [[insignificant]] against such a vast problem. Additionally, our entire economic system is built around consumption, making unsustainable choices the default. So it is a combination of practical obstacles, [[ingrained habits]] and a sense of [[powerlessness]].

Businesses have a huge role to play. They can reduce their carbon footprint by using renewable energy and improving efficiency. Adopting [[circular economy]] principles, where products are designed to be reused and recycled, cuts waste dramatically. [[Sourcing]] materials ethically and being transparent about their impact matters too. Crucially, they should see sustainability not as a cost but as an investment that can drive innovation and win loyalty from increasingly [[conscious consumers]].

I am hopeful they will, partly [[out of necessity]]. As the impacts of unsustainable living become more severe, future generations will likely be forced to adapt. [[Encouragingly]], young people today already show strong environmental values and are pushing for change. Advances in green technology should also make sustainable living easier and cheaper. So I believe sustainability will increasingly become the norm rather than the exception, driven by both necessity and [[shifting values]].
fixes.why: 'norm' and 'necessity' are plain; marked 'out of necessity', 'encouragingly', 'shifting values'

fixes.answer: Governments have powerful tools [[at their disposal]]. They can use financial incentives, like subsidies for renewable energy or electric cars, and taxes on pollution and waste to [[steer behaviour]]. Investing in sustainable infrastructure, such as public transport and recycling, makes green choices easier. Regulation and clear information, like [[carbon labelling]], also help. Essentially, by making the sustainable choice the easy, affordable and default option, governments can drive widespread change.
fixes.why: 'easy', 'affordable', 'change' are plain; marked 'at their disposal', 'steer behaviour', 'carbon labelling'

fixes.answer: Recycling has clear advantages: it [[conserves]] natural resources, reduces landfill waste, saves energy compared to making new products, and cuts pollution. It also raises environmental awareness. The disadvantages are that the process itself consumes energy and water, some materials are difficult or costly to recycle, and [[contamination]] can [[render efforts ineffective]]. So while recycling is genuinely beneficial, it is not a complete solution and works best alongside reducing and reusing.
fixes.why: 'beneficial' and 'reusing' are plain; marked 'conserves', 'contamination', 'render efforts ineffective'

fixes.answer: There is some truth to this currently, though it is changing. It is true that some sustainable products, like organic food or electric cars, carry a higher [[price tag]], which can put them [[out of reach]] for those on tight budgets. This is a real barrier to [[widespread adoption]]. However, as demand grows and technology improves, prices are steadily falling. So while cost is a genuine obstacle today, I believe sustainability is becoming increasingly affordable and accessible.
fixes.why: 'obstacle', 'affordable', 'accessible' are plain; marked 'price tag', 'out of reach', 'widespread adoption'
